turns.prompt_text: What do you use to clean a cast iron skillet
turns.response_html:
Cleaning cast iron is remarkably straightforward once you bypass the old myths. The entire process hinges on protecting the seasoning—that slick, polymerized layer of oil baked onto the metal—while completely removing food residue.

Here is the ideal toolkit and the exact method to keep it in peak condition.

The Toolkit

  • Warm water
  • A stiff-bristled brush or a chainmail scrubber
  • Mild dish soap (Modern dish soaps are perfectly safe; the old "no soap" rule stems from the days when soaps contained harsh lye, which is no longer the case)
  • Kosher salt (An excellent, non-destructive abrasive for stubborn, charred bits)
  • A high-smoke-point oil (Canola, grapeseed, or vegetable oil)

The Cleaning Sequence

The Cast Iron Rules: Never leave the skillet soaking in the sink, never run it through the dishwasher, and avoid using harsh acids like vinegar or lemon juice for routine cleaning, as they can break down the seasoned surface layer over time.

It works in a pinch for a quick post-wash maintenance wipe, but it is far from ideal if you want to build a durable, slick, non-stick seasoning layer.

Here is why coconut oil struggles with cast iron, broken down by the science of the pan:

1. The Saturated Fat Problem

Building a true "seasoning" requires polymerization—a process where liquid oil transforms into a hard, plastic-like protective coating by cross-linking its molecules under high heat.

  • Oils high in polyunsaturated fats (like grapeseed, canola, or sunflower oil) have molecular structures that excel at cross-linking.
  • Coconut oil is roughly 80% to 90% saturated fat. Because its molecular chains are already fully saturated, they don't link up effectively. Instead of baking into a tough, slick shield, coconut oil tends to leave a coating that can feel soft, sticky, or gummy over time.

2. Smoke Point Discrepancies

If you do use coconut oil, the type matters immensely due to its smoke point:

  • Unrefined (Virgin) Coconut Oil: Has a low smoke point of around 350°F. If you heat your skillet past this point during normal cooking, the oil will break down, burn off, and smoke heavily, which degrades whatever seasoning you have. Plus, it will make your kitchen smell like a tropical vacation.
  • Refined Coconut Oil: Is processed to remove impurities, bumping its smoke point up to a much safer 400°F to 450°F. It is completely neutral in flavor and odor.

The Verdict: If you use your skillet every single day, wiping a microscopic layer of refined coconut oil onto the pan after washing will protect it from moisture and rust just fine. But if you are trying to build up that legendary, mirror-smooth non-stick finish, you are much better off sticking to grapeseed, canola, or Crisco.

Olive oil is a step up from coconut oil for basic maintenance, but it still isn't ideal for building a long-term seasoning layer. In fact, using the wrong type of olive oil can actually ruin a pan's finish.

The breakdown depends entirely on how the olive oil was processed:

The Problem with Extra Virgin Olive Oil (EVOO)

Extra Virgin olive oil is unrefined, meaning it still contains microscopic bits of actual olive fruit pulp and organic compounds.

  • Low Smoke Point: EVOO begins to smoke and break down at a relatively low 325°F to 375°F.
  • The "Sticky Carbon" Effect: When you heat EVOO to its smoke point, those organic fruit solids burn, char, and turn into a sticky, flaky, bitter-tasting layer of carbon instead of a smooth, slick polymer. If your pan feels gummy or has black flakes coming off in your food, EVOO is often the culprit.

Refined (Light or Pure) Olive Oil is Okay

If the label says "Light," "Pure," or just "Olive Oil," it has been refined to strip away those fruit solids.

  • This pushes the smoke point up significantly to around 410°F to 460°F.
  • Because it is neutral and can handle heat, refined olive oil works perfectly fine for a quick wipe after you wash and dry the skillet.

The Chemistry: Monounsaturated Fats

Chemically, olive oil is primarily a monounsaturated fat. Remember how polyunsaturated fats (canola, grapeseed) excel at cross-linking into a durable "plastic" layer, and saturated fats (coconut) barely link at all? Monounsaturated fats sit right in the middle. They will polymerize, but it takes a lot longer and the resulting coating isn't quite as tough or scratch-resistant.

The Cupboard Warning: If you cook with your cast iron every single day, refined olive oil is fine for maintenance. However, if you store your skillet in a cupboard for weeks at a time, olive oil can oxidize and go rancid, leaving you with a sticky, foul-smelling pan the next time you pull it out.

turns.prompt_text: What is the best low-cost oil I should use for a cast iron skillet?
turns.response_html:
Here is the beautiful secret about cast iron: the absolute best oils for building a tough, slick seasoning layer also happen to be the cheapest ones on the grocery shelf.

You don't need fancy specialty oils. In fact, expensive options like avocado oil or flaxseed oil either have a smoke point that is too high to easily polymerize, or they tend to crack and flake off over time.

For the perfect balance of performance and budget, stick to these three low-cost champions:

Oil / FatSmoke PointPrice PointWhy It Wins
Canola Oil~400°FExtremely LowThe absolute easiest daily driver. It has the ideal ratio of unsaturated fats to link up into a slick coating, it's completely neutral, and it costs pennies.
Vegetable Oil~400°F to 450°FExtremely LowUsually made from 100% soybean oil. It performs almost identically to canola oil and is highly effective at building up a dark, durable finish.
Crisco (Vegetable Shortening)~490°FVery LowThe old-school, multi-generational favorite. Because it's a solid at room temperature, it won't run or leave sticky pools if you accidentally apply a bit too much.

The Budget Pick

If you want one bottle that sits under the sink exclusively for cast iron maintenance, go with a basic bottle of Canola Oil.

After you wash and dry your skillet on the stovetop, just put a nickel-sized drop in the pan, rub it completely all over with a paper towel until the pan looks dry and matte, and you're good to go. A standard 48-ounce bottle will easily last you a few years.

turns.prompt_text: I have vegetable oil but it sounds like I need canola oil
turns.response_html:
You definitely don't need to run out and buy a new bottle! The vegetable oil you already have in your pantry is perfect for the job.

You can stick with what you've got for a few reasons:

  • It is practically the same thing: If you check the ingredient label on your vegetable oil, 99% of the time it just says "100% Soybean Oil." In the world of cast iron chemistry, soybean oil and canola oil are essentially siblings.
  • It excels at seasoning: Soybean oil is packed with polyunsaturated fats, meaning it will cross-link and bake into that tough, slick, non-stick shield just as well as canola oil will.
  • High heat tolerance: Its smoke point is right around 400°F to 450°F, which is the sweet spot for taking stovetop heat without burning off or breaking down into a sticky mess.

Save your cash and use what is already on hand.

Just remember the golden rule of cast iron maintenance: less is more. After washing and drying your skillet on the stove, put a tiny, nickel-sized drop of your vegetable oil in the pan. Rub it all over the surface with a paper towel, and then immediately take a fresh, dry paper towel and buff the pan until it looks completely matte.

If it looks shiny or wet, there is too much oil left on the surface, which can turn gummy or sticky before your next meal. You want to wipe it down until it feels like you accidentally wiped all the oil off—that microscopic layer left behind is all the metal needs.
